imperial.name: Pea

actions.text:
Sow

Mid-Mar–early May. In mild areas, hardy round-seeded peas can overwinter from a protected Nov sowing.

methods.text:
Sow 

Make a flat-bottomed drill about 4 in. wide and 2 in. deep. Scatter the peas across its width, cover and firm gently. Protect from birds.

Under cover 

If the ground is cold, start peas in modules under glass. Plant out with the roots intact once the bed is workable. Put pea sticks or mesh in place before stems sprawl.

Pea.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer

Peas are a reward of early summer: freshly picked pods are sweet, but sugars soon turn to starch. Although long grown for canning, freezing and drying, home-grown peas taste best picked young and eaten or cooked at once.

Quick facts
Harvest

Jun – Jul

Germination

7–10 days

Sowing depth

About 2 in. for garden peas

Yield (10 ft row)

10 lb

Ready in

From sowing: spring crops 12–16 weeks; autumn crops ~32 weeks

Sow

Mid-Mar–early May. In mild areas, hardy round-seeded peas can overwinter from a protected Nov sowing.

Row spacing

Tall rows/supports: about 5 ft apart; closer for dwarfs/beds.

Seed spacing

1–2 in. apart in drills.

Recommended varieties
WRINKLED
Kelvedon Wonder

Compact early shelling pea for small spaces and early harvests. Give short supports.

WRINKLED
Hurst Green Shaft

Familiar maincrop shelling pea with long pods for generous pickings.

MANGETOUT
Oregon Sugar Pod

Whole, flat mangetout pods: pick before peas swell for tenderness.

SUGAR SNAP
Sugar Ann

Early sugar-snap pea with crisp, edible pods, contrasting with shelling and mangetout.

WRINKLED
Alderman

Tall shelling pea; strong supports and extra height reward with longer picking.

ROUND
Meteor

A compact round-seeded pea for colder or exposed sites. Useful for early crops.

ROUND
Douce Provence

A sweet, round-seeded pea with robust growth.

MANGETOUT
Norli

Compact mangetout with sweet, flat pods. Pick while the peas inside are tiny.

Key risks
Pea moth / caterpillars

The most obvious pea problem is caterpillars inside pods, eating the peas.

Mildew

Mildew often appears from about the second week of July onwards, especially on late sowings or in damp, muggy weather.

Birds

Birds eat seed and seedlings and may peck leaves.

Mice

Mice may take the large edible seeds before germination.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
74
PEAS & BEANS

Support and protect peas early.

Guard newly sown rows against birds and provide supports before plants sprawl.

Water when flowers and pods form.

Moisture at this stage helps produce a useful, tender crop.

Soil & preparation
Use compost-rich, moist but well-drained soil. Avoid cold, waterlogging and heavy nitrogen feeds.
Sowing & planting
Sow a broad drill
Cover and support
Sow 

Make a flat-bottomed drill about 4 in. wide and 2 in. deep. Scatter the peas across its width, cover and firm gently. Protect from birds.

Under cover 

If the ground is cold, start peas in modules under glass. Plant out with the roots intact once the bed is workable. Put pea sticks or mesh in place before stems sprawl.

Looking after the crop
Support early with pea sticks or secure netting; weed and guard young plants. Short twiggy sticks keep dwarf pods clear of dirt and slugs. Give tall varieties strong supports before stems sprawl.
Water as flowers and pods form; mulch and leave healthy roots after cropping. Supports improve airflow. Avoid wet foliage, especially in hot, muggy weather when mildew spreads.
Harvesting & storage
Pick shelling peas full but sweet, mangetout flat, and snap peas plump but crisp. Work regularly from the bottom up, holding the vine with one hand as you pick with the other. Ripening pods slow further cropping.
Use a separate sowing for shoots. Let drying peas or suitable seed mature fully; finish drying under cover in wet weather.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Pea moth / caterpillars	Caterpillars inside pods.	Sow early; mesh before flowering.
Mildew	White powder on leaves or pods.	Resistant varieties; water roots, space well.
Birds	Seeds or young leaves taken.	Protect with taut netting or wire guards.
Mice	Seed vanishes before sprouting.	Use protected modules or seed guards.
Slugs	Young plants or low pods chewed.	Support early; check and hand-pick.
Pea and bean weevil	U-shaped leaf-edge notches.	Protect seedlings; light damage is tolerated.
Pea thrips	Tiny insects; silvery damage.	Confirm pest; water, tolerate minor damage.
Pea aphid	Colonies on tender shoots.	Squash damaging clusters; favour predators.
Downy mildew	Yellow patches; mould beneath.	Remove affected leaves; improve airflow.
Foot rot and root rot	Yellowing; roots and base rot.	Remove affected plants; drain and rotate.
Final tips

Start early crops under cover and sow short rows in succession for manageable pickings.

Pick frequently: pods left to mature can slow further cropping.

VEGETABLE GUIDES

amendments.sourceNote: John requests a round-seeded variety and removal of the deep-bed instruction from Seed spacing. Add Meteor, already a rank-6 Round varieties entry, without replacing the existing five selections or changing master ranks. Its compact habit and suitability for cold/exposed sites come from the master; round seed and earliness are confirmed by current seed suppliers. Heights are omitted because suppliers differ from the master; no canonical measurements change. There are no pH or liming references in this working spread. Original page-2 copy, ten pest rows and artwork remain.
amendments.varietyExpansionNote: John asks whether more varieties will fit. Add two rank-6 selections from the existing master: Douce Provence for sweetness and robust growth, and Norli for compact mangetout. Keep all six existing entries and use two rows of four at unchanged type sizes. Preliminary DOM trials in both units found nine entries in the three-column design overflowed by 8.78 mm; eight in four columns left 7.12 mm above the footer. The scoped column override does not alter other crops.
